rendered:
This review never mentions that organism, so it offers no comparison with it. A search of every line, cell, caption, OCR line and figure fact finds neither the genus nor the species name anywhere in the document.[1]

What the document does benchmark S. marcescens against are the mature model hosts. The introduction frames metabolic engineering as having relied onmicroorganisms such as Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae[2], whose limits it lists as[3]restricted substrate utilization spectra, insufficient adaptability to complex environmental conditions, and the lack of native pathways required for the biosynthesis of certain complex natural products[4]. The only other non-model host named as an illustration of ecological advantage is a halophile genus:Halomonas exhibit high salt and alkali tolerance and strong resistance to microbial contamination, enabling open and non-sterile fermentation[5].

Against the model hosts, S. marcescens is argued to win on tolerance and on product compatibility rather than on genetic maturity. Strain HBQA7 grows in geraniol concentrations that strongly inhibit the enterobacterial model host, and[6]tolerates up to 2 M methanol[7]. In terpenoid work the comparison is quantitative: for cineole the authors report[8]with space–time yields exceeding E. coli and S. cerevisiae[9], and for a polyamine the engineered strain gave[10]outperforming E. coli BL21(DE3)[11]. The positioning section generalizes this: hydrophobic terpenoids[12]cause membrane toxicity in E. coli and S. cerevisiae, whereas S. marcescens exhibits superior host-product compatibility[13].

On the deficit side, the review is explicit thatcompared to mature industrial chassis, S. marcescens remains in the early stages of development[14], constrained by[15]biosafety concerns, scalability and fermentation compatibility, and product economics[16]. Hence the strategic conclusion is complementarity, not substitution:Rather than directly competing with highly optimized traditional chassis like E. coli and S. cerevisiae, S. marcescens must leverage its unique physiological traits to establish differentiated competitiveness[17], and in the abstract,S. marcescens is positioned not to replace traditional model hosts, but to serve as a specialized, ecologically robust platform[18].

The criteria the review uses to judge any chassis are stated generally, so they could in principle be applied to other non-model hosts even though none beyond those named above are evaluated here:An effective industrial chassis must satisfy four key criteria: (i) robust growth and stress tolerance (e.g., temperature, pH, osmotic pressure, product toxicity) under industrial conditions; (ii) utilization of inexpensive, renewable feedstocks; (iii) metabolic versatility for native or heterologous biosynthesis; and (iv) a mature genetic toolbox for precise engineering[19]. Evidence for S. marcescens under these headings is collected in its substrate profile,Table 1[20], its engineered product portfolio,Table 2[21], and its tool set,Fig. 6[22].
